overview: Struthiosaurus (meaning 'ostrich lizard') was a small nodosaurid ankylosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Europe, living approximately 83–75 million years ago. It reached about 2.5 metres in length — considerably smaller than most ankylosaurs — and has been found across a wide area including Austria, France, Romania, and Spain. Named by Bunzel in 1871, it is one of the oldest scientifically described ankylosaurs and the best-known ankylosaur from Europe.

The diminutive size of Struthiosaurus is widely attributed to insular dwarfism: during the Late Cretaceous, much of what is now central and southern Europe was an archipelago of islands in the Tethys Sea, and island populations frequently evolve reduced body sizes due to limited resources. Struthiosaurus was likely protected by bony armour including cervical half-rings and dorsal osteoderms, compensating for its small stature against predators. Its long taxonomic history is complicated by fragmentary material from multiple localities.

fossilSites.name: Gosau Group deposits
fossilSites.note: The type specimen of S. austriacus was recovered from Gosau Formation deposits in the Austrian Alps, representing Late Cretaceous island environments.

fossilSites.name: Hateg Basin (Sânpetru Formation)
fossilSites.note: Struthiosaurus transylvanicus from the Hateg Basin is the best-known European ankylosaur, from an island ecosystem famous for its dwarf dinosaurs.

fossilSites.name: Iberian Late Cretaceous beds
fossilSites.note: Spanish material attributed to Struthiosaurus comes from continental Late Cretaceous deposits, consistent with an island-hopping distribution across the European archipelago.

articles.title: Discovery and Naming
articles.body: Struthiosaurus austriacus was named by Emmanuel Bunzel in 1871 from fragmentary material collected in the Gosau Formation of Austria — one of the earliest Cretaceous dinosaur descriptions from central Europe. The odd name 'ostrich lizard' likely reflects early misinterpretation of the material. Subsequent discoveries in Romania, France, and Spain have expanded the genus, though the validity of some referred species remains debated.

articles.title: Insular Dwarfism
articles.body: At roughly 2.5 metres, Struthiosaurus was about half the length of continental North American nodosaurids such as Edmontonia. This size reduction is almost certainly the result of island dwarfism — the well-documented evolutionary trend in which island-dwelling animals evolve smaller body sizes over generations when resources are limited and large predators are absent. The Hateg Basin of Romania has yielded multiple dwarf dinosaurs, including a dwarf sauropod (Magyarosaurus), underscoring the insular nature of Late Cretaceous European environments.

articles.title: Armour and Defence
articles.body: Despite its small size, Struthiosaurus retained the armour characteristic of nodosaurids: bony cervical half-rings protecting the neck, dorsal osteoderms along the back, and likely lateral spines. As a nodosaurid, it lacked the tail club of ankylosaurids but compensated with passive armour. The precise arrangement of armour elements is uncertain because articulated specimens are rare.

articles.title: European Archipelago Fauna
articles.body: The Late Cretaceous European archipelago was home to a distinctive 'Hateg Island' fauna characterised by dwarfed dinosaurs (Magyarosaurus, Zalmoxes, Struthiosaurus), unusual crocodilians, and giant pterosaurs such as Hatzegopteryx. Struthiosaurus was part of this unique insular ecosystem, which provides a natural experiment in understanding how isolation shapes evolutionary trajectories.

record.description: Struthiosaurus was a small European nodosaurid represented by three named species and numerous fragmentary specimens from Austria, Hungary, Romania and France.
facts: No single specimen supplies a complete skeleton.
Genus-level range and anatomy are composites across geographically separated species; a Santonian Hungarian humerus was referred only as cf. Struthiosaurus.

review.ageReviewNote: Named species are Campanian-Maastrichtian, while a cf. Struthiosaurus humerus may extend the record into the Santonian.

sources.citation: Ősi & Prondvai (2013), a Santonian humerus referred to cf. Struthiosaurus

residualUncertainty: Species boundaries and the Santonian referral remain difficult.

evidence.material: Multiple fragmentary skull and postcranial specimens across three species, plus a Santonian humerus referred as cf. Struthiosaurus.
evidence.formations: Several Santonian-Maastrichtian units in central and western Europe.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Do not merge all species into one complete 2.5 m individual or treat the Santonian referral as certain.
evidence.summary: Struthiosaurus was a small European nodosaurid represented by three named species and numerous fragmentary specimens from Austria, Hungary, Romania and France.
